final_codebook.domain: Subtracting fractions, mixed numbers, and whole numbers with simplification

skills.name: Align fractional forms
skills.definition: Rewrite quantities into compatible forms for subtraction, including finding common denominators, converting to equivalent fractions, rewriting a whole number with a zero fractional part, and normalizing a mixed number with an improper fractional part.
inclusion_criteria: Tag when a step finds an LCD or common denominator before subtraction.
Tag when a fraction is converted to an equivalent fraction with the new denominator.
Tag when a whole number is rewritten as a whole plus 0 over a denominator to align with a fraction or mixed number.
Tag when a mixed number with an improper fractional part is rewritten as an equivalent standard mixed number before subtraction.
exclusion_criteria: Do not tag when denominators are already the same and no preparatory rewriting is performed.
Do not tag the arithmetic subtraction of already-aligned whole or fractional parts.
Do not tag borrowing or regrouping after subtraction has begun.
Do not tag final reduction or formatting of the answer.

skills.name: Subtract aligned parts
skills.definition: Carry out subtraction once the quantities are in compatible form, including subtracting numerators of like-denominator fractions and subtracting whole-number and fractional parts of mixed numbers when no regrouping is performed in that step.
inclusion_criteria: Tag when the solution subtracts numerators of fractions that already share a denominator.
Tag when the solution subtracts whole-number parts of mixed numbers or rewritten whole numbers.
Tag when the solution separately subtracts whole and fractional parts after any needed alignment has been completed.
exclusion_criteria: Do not tag denominator-finding, equivalent-fraction conversion, whole-number rewriting, or mixed-number normalization steps.
Do not tag borrowing or regrouping steps that adjust the whole and fractional parts after a negative fractional result appears.
Do not tag simplification or final recombination alone.

skills.name: Borrow across parts
skills.definition: Regroup by taking 1 from the whole-number part and converting it into fractional units so subtraction can continue when the fractional part would otherwise be negative.
inclusion_criteria: Tag when the solution explicitly borrows 1 from the whole part.
Tag when the borrowed 1 is converted to denominator-over-denominator or equivalent fractional units and added to the existing fractional part.
Tag when subtraction is recomputed using the regrouped fractional part.
exclusion_criteria: Do not tag ordinary subtraction when no regrouping is needed.
Do not tag initial rewriting of a whole number as a whole plus 0 over a denominator unless the step actually performs borrowing.
Do not tag final simplification or combining of already-computed parts.

skills.name: Simplify and express result
skills.definition: Reduce the computed difference to lowest terms and present it in an appropriate final form such as a fraction, mixed number, whole number, or 0.
inclusion_criteria: Tag when the solution simplifies a fraction to lowest terms.
Tag when 0 over a denominator is rewritten as 0 or when a zero fractional part is removed.
Tag when whole and fractional parts are combined into the final reported mixed number, fraction, whole number, or 0.
exclusion_criteria: Do not tag the arithmetic subtraction itself.
Do not tag denominator alignment, equivalent-fraction conversion, or mixed-number normalization steps.
Do not tag borrowing or regrouping unless the step's main purpose is the final simplified expression.

decisions.reasoning: This candidate had 3/3 consensus and captures a broad but coherent preparation process that is independently testable from subtraction, borrowing, and simplification. It also covers multiple observed dossier steps such as common-denominator conversion and rewriting whole numbers with zero fractional parts.

Normalize mixed numbers appeared in only 1 expert codebook and fewer than 3-4 items as a distinct operation. In the dossiers, it functions as a special case of preparatory rewriting before subtraction, not a separate downstream process. Keeping it separate would reduce minimality and create a narrow skill with weak identifiability.

This candidate had 3/3 consensus and is clearly distinct from preparation, regrouping, and simplification. It is independently testable across many items where subtraction occurs without borrowing or reduction.

Although only 2/3 experts separated borrowing, dossier evidence shows it is a distinct cognitive operation that does not always co-occur with simplification. Separating it improves diagnostic resolution because some items require regrouping without any nontrivial reduction, while others require simplification without regrouping.

This candidate is distinct from subtraction and regrouping and appears in multiple items as a final reduction or expression step. It supports clarity of boundaries and preserves the A/C distinction between doing the arithmetic and formatting the final answer.

decisions.details: Removed C06 as a standalone candidate
decisions.reasoning: C06 combines two cognitively different operations: regrouping and final simplification. Because these do not always co-occur and are independently testable in the dossiers, keeping them merged would violate non-redundancy and reduce diagnostic usefulness. Its coverage is preserved by S03 and S04.

decisions.details: Refined all retained skill definitions and criteria to clarify boundaries between alignment, subtraction, borrowing, and final expression
decisions.reasoning: The expert codebooks differed mainly in granularity and boundary wording. Refinement was needed to ensure independent annotators can consistently distinguish preparatory rewriting from regrouping, and arithmetic subtraction from final simplification.

summary: The final codebook adopts the four-skill structure most strongly supported by the dossiers and by experts A and C: preparation/alignment, subtraction, borrowing, and simplification. The only major consolidation choice was folding improper mixed-number normalization into alignment, because it is a narrow special case of preparatory rewriting rather than a stable standalone skill. Expert B's combined regroup-and-simplify skill was split conceptually into borrowing and simplification to preserve independence, completeness, and better Q-matrix identifiability.
